title: Forgive, or fight back?
hook: in the forest, Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for kshama, forgiveness, and Prahlada's old answer weighs both
carry: kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour
tomorrow: they were cheated. why keep the promise?

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where Draupadi told her friend Krishna everything, and he heard her to the end. Your line was sakhya: you can tell God everything.

An evening in the forest, and a married couple is having a real argument. Draupadi looks at her husband in his bark clothes, sleeping on the ground, and she can't stand it. You were a king, she says. Your brothers are suffering. How is your anger not blazing? Yudhishthira doesn't storm out. He answers her, at length. And she answers back. The epic doesn't cut the scene short or tell us who won. It gives both of them the floor.
screen: `A COUPLE ARGUES IN THE FOREST.` → `WHY IS YOUR ANGER NOT BLAZING?` → `BOTH OF THEM GET THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't argue from feeling alone. She brings a story. Long ago, she says, the demon king Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada, the same Prahlada whose verdict Vidura told in the hall: which is better, forgiveness or might? Prahlada answered: neither one, always. Someone who forgives everything is treated with contempt, even by his own servants. Someone who never forgives makes enemies of everyone. There's a time for each, and wisdom is knowing which time it is. Now, says Draupadi, is the time for might. Yudhishthira answers with a different picture. Anger, he says, is the root of destruction; an angry person can't tell what should be said from what shouldn't. Forgiveness holds the world together. He calls it the strength of the strong. The word he praises is kshama: forgiveness, patience under wrong, and old Hindu lists of the marks of dharma include it. So who is right? Here's the teaching the scene leaves you with. Kshama is a real strength, not a weakness. But Prahlada adds the word that keeps it honest: time. Dharma isn't one rule for every moment; it reads the hour. Is the person sorry? Is this the first time? Would forgiving now protect anyone, or only let the harm go on? Draupadi isn't the hothead, and Yudhishthira isn't the saint. Both quote their tradition. That's why, in many Hindu homes, 'forgive' and 'stand up for yourself' can both be dharma. The wisdom is knowing which hour it is.
screen: `PRAHLADA: A TIME FOR EACH.` · `DRAUPADI: NOW IS THE TIME FOR MIGHT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: KSHAMA IS STRENGTH.` · then, large: `DHARMA READS THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one wrong someone did you, a medium one, not the biggest. Breathe in with Draupadi's question: is this a time for strength? Breathe out with Yudhishthira's: what would carrying this anger do to me? Then ask Prahlada's: what does this hour call for? If you pray, ask for kshama, and for the wisdom to know its time; if not, just let the three questions sit.
Vana. The forest of exile, where Draupadi argues for might and Yudhishthira for kshama, and both are heard.
Your line: kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour. Prahlada's answer was that each has its time. Tomorrow: they were cheated, so why keep the promise? That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 779 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THEY WERE CHEATED. WHY KEEP THE PROMISE?`

howItsDone: Teachers and commentators return to this forest debate between Draupadi and Yudhishthira when discussing anger, kshama (forgiveness) and right action, and Prahlada's answer to Bali, a time for each, is retold on its own as well.

fork.setup: a classmate tore down your posters, then came and said sorry. with Prahlada's answer in mind, what fits?
options: forgive him, and speak up if it happens again.
never forgive; forgivers get walked on.
forgive everything, every time, no matter what.
fork.reveal: Prahlada: neither one always. kshama is strength, but dharma reads the hour, and a real first apology is a time to forgive.

original.note: Sanskrit kshama: forgiveness, patience under wrong.

chat.meaning: Prahlada told Bali that always forgiving brings contempt and never forgiving makes enemies: there's a time for each. Kshama is strength, and dharma reads the hour.

Prahlada.meaning: Bali's grandfather, whose fair verdict Vidura told in the hall

Yudhishthira.meaning: the eldest Pandava brother, now in exile

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the dialogue of Draupadi and Yudhishthira in the forest (Draupadi's reproach; the conversation of Prahlada and Bali; Yudhishthira on anger and forgiveness)
Manusmriti 6.92 (the ten marks of dharma, which include kshama, forgiveness)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli that Draupadi tells the Prahlada and Bali (Vali) conversation, and the gist of Prahlada's answer (neither always forgiveness nor always might; contempt for the always-forgiving).
Confirm Yudhishthira's points: anger as the root of destruction; the angry cannot tell what should be said; forgiveness keeps peace among creatures; 'the might of the mighty' or similar.
Ganguli's text includes verses attributed to Kashyapa praising forgiveness; left out because exact wording isn't certain.
The later part of the debate (Draupadi on why the good suffer, Yudhishthira on acting without seeking reward) is left for another day or for a Keeper's choice.
